name: Dense Deposit Disease (Membranoproliferative Glomerulonephritis Type II)

clinicalPearls: A subtype of C3 glomerulopathy driven by dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, with characteristic osmiophilic intramembranous dense deposits transforming the glomerular basement membrane on electron microscopy.
Immunofluorescence shows dominant C3 deposition with little or no immunoglobulin, distinguishing it from immune-complex membranoproliferative patterns.
Commonly presents in children and young adults with a nephritic-nephrotic overlap: haematuria, proteinuria, oedema and variable hypertension.
Serum C3 is often persistently depressed while C4 remains normal, reflecting isolated alternative-pathway consumption.
C3 nephritic factor, an autoantibody that stabilises the alternative-pathway C3 convertase, is frequently detectable and perpetuates uncontrolled C3 breakdown.
Associated systemic features include acquired partial lipodystrophy and ocular drusen resembling those of age-related macular degeneration.
Screen for acquired and inherited complement abnormalities, including factor H deficiency or autoantibodies and pathogenic complement gene variants.
Disease tends to recur in kidney allografts, so complement evaluation and counselling should precede transplantation.
reference.pathophysiology: Dense deposit disease results from unrestrained activation of the alternative complement pathway within the fluid phase, most often perpetuated by C3 nephritic factor, an autoantibody that binds and stabilises the alternative-pathway C3 convertase and renders it resistant to normal decay. Less commonly the dysregulation arises from autoantibodies to factor H or factor B, from acquired factor H deficiency, or from pathogenic variants in complement regulatory genes. The resulting continuous cleavage of C3 generates activation fragments that are deposited along and within the glomerular basement membrane, mesangium and Bowman capsule, producing the pathognomonic ribbon-like, intensely electron-dense transformation of the lamina densa. Because activation is confined largely to the alternative pathway, the classical-pathway component C4 is characteristically spared while C3 is consumed. The deposited complement drives mesangial and endocapillary proliferation, capillary wall remodelling with a membranoproliferative light-microscopic appearance, and progressive glomerular injury. The same systemic complement dysregulation underlies the extrarenal manifestations, with complement-laden deposits accumulating in adipose tissue to cause partial lipodystrophy and in Bruch membrane of the retina to form drusen.
additionalDifferentials: C3 glomerulonephritis (the other C3 glomerulopathy subtype, with mesangial and subendothelial rather than intramembranous dense deposits)
Immune-complex membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (immunoglobulin plus complement on immunofluorescence)
Post-infectious glomerulonephritis, which can also show low C3 but typically resolves
Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (shared alternative-pathway dysregulation with thrombotic microangiopathy)
Monoclonal gammopathy-associated C3 glomerulopathy in older adults
Lupus nephritis with a membranoproliferative pattern
additionalInvestigations: Renal biopsy with light microscopy, immunofluorescence and electron microscopy to confirm intramembranous dense deposits and C3-dominant staining
Serum C3, C4 and alternative-pathway complement profiling
Assay for C3 nephritic factor and other complement autoantibodies including anti-factor H and anti-factor B
Complement gene panel for regulatory variants (CFH, CFI, CFB, C3, CFHR genes)
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with free light chains to exclude monoclonal gammopathy, especially in older patients
Quantification of proteinuria and monitoring of renal function
redFlags: Rapidly rising creatinine or crescents on biopsy suggesting a rapidly progressive course
Nephrotic-range proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia and progressive oedema
Features of thrombotic microangiopathy overlapping with atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome
Recurrence with graft dysfunction after kidney transplantation
New monoclonal protein in an older patient indicating gammopathy-driven disease
reference.prognosis: Dense deposit disease carries a guarded long-term prognosis, with a substantial proportion of patients progressing to kidney failure over one to two decades despite treatment. Recurrence in the transplanted kidney is common and frequently threatens graft survival.
pitfalls: Labelling all membranoproliferative patterns as immune-complex disease without electron microscopy, thereby missing the C3-dominant dense deposit picture
Assuming a normal C3 excludes the diagnosis, as complement levels can fluctuate or normalise
Overlooking the systemic associations of lipodystrophy and retinal drusen
Failing to screen for monoclonal gammopathy in older adults with C3 glomerulopathy
Proceeding to transplantation without complement evaluation given the high recurrence risk
references: Brenner and Rector's The Kidney (standard reference)
Consensus guidance on C3 glomerulopathy (standard reference)
